area: Area V. Performance and Ground Reference Maneuvers
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how a lazy eight trades airspeed for altitude and back, why rudder and aileron pressures never stop changing, and fly symmetrical loops that pass the commercial standard (about 30° of bank at the steepest point; altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots and heading ±10° at each 180° point).
why: The lazy eight builds coordination of the flight controls across a wide range of airspeeds and attitudes, and it is the only standard training maneuver in which control pressures are always changing [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. It is also a lesson in energy: speed turns into altitude and back again, the same exchange that, mismanaged, feeds loss of control and CFIT accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

prereading.what: The lazy eight: shape, the 45°, 90° and 135° reference points, rudder use, entry speed and power, and the common errors. Read this twice.
prereading.label: AFH 10-6 to 10-7

prereading.what: Energy management: potential and kinetic energy, thrust minus drag, and trading airspeed for altitude.
prereading.label: AFH 4-1 to 4-3

prereading.what: The energy map, energy height, and the three rules for using throttle and elevator together.
prereading.label: AFH 4-7 to 4-10

prereading.what: Classes of turns, lift components, adverse yaw, and how a slip and a skid feel.
prereading.label: AFH 3-12 to 3-13

prereading.what: P-factor, load factors, the PHAK note on chandelles and lazy eights, and the Vg diagram.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-32 to 5-38

prereading.what: Accelerated stalls, VA and VO, recovery, and the cross-control stall.
prereading.label: AFH 5-19 to 5-20

prereading.what: Airspeed indicator markings and the limits that are not marked, including VA and how it changes with weight.
prereading.label: PHAK 8-9 to 8-10

warmup: Think first: in a lazy eight you never touch the throttle, yet the airspeed swings from cruise to a few knots above the stall and back, and you finish at the same altitude you started. Where does the speed go at the top, and what would have to be true about your power setting for you to land back on your entry altitude every time?

key_terms.def: Two linked 180° turns in opposite directions, each with a climb in its first 90° and a descent in its second 90°, so the nose draws an eight lying on its side across the horizon [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].
Prominent points on the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135° from the direction each 180° turn starts, used to make the loops symmetrical [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
The top of each loop: bank about 30°, minimum airspeed about 5 to 10 knots above stall speed, and the pitch attitude passing through level [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].
Planning, monitoring and controlling altitude and airspeed in relation to the airplane's energy state [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Potential energy from altitude plus kinetic energy from airspeed, written mgh + ½mV² [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].
Trading airspeed for altitude or altitude for airspeed. With no other inputs the two always move in opposite directions [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].
Altitude plus V² / 2g: the greatest height the airplane could reach by trading all its speed for altitude [[24:93|AFH 4-7]] [[24:94|AFH 4-8]].
The yaw away from the turn caused by the extra drag on the rising wing when you deflect the ailerons; rudder cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].
At a high angle of attack the downward-moving propeller blade takes a bigger bite, which yaws the nose to the left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
Any stall that happens with more than +1 G on the airplane, so it comes at a higher indicated airspeed than the normal stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
A graph of load factor against airspeed that shows the safe envelope: the stall lines, the limit load factor and the redline [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]].
Flying by outside references with quick instrument cross-checks: about 90 percent of attention outside, no more than about 10 percent inside [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

chunks.title: The lazy eight at commercial standards

body.p: Think of S-turns across a road: a 180° turn one way, then a 180° turn the other way. A lazy eight adds a climb and a descent to each 180°. The first 90° of each half is a climb and the second 90° is a descent [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

From the cockpit, imagine the airplane's longitudinal axis is a pencil. As you fly both 180° turns, the nose draws a symmetrical eight lying on its side, with parts above and below the horizon. It takes both turns to draw both loops [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. The maneuver exists to build smooth, coordinated control over a wide band of airspeeds and attitudes [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Select an altitude that allows the maneuver to be performed no lower than 1,500 feet above ground level (AGL) (ACS CA.V.D.S2)
Establish the recommended entry configuration, power, and airspeed (ACS CA.V.D.S3)
Maintain coordinated flight throughout the maneuver (ACS CA.V.D.S4)
Approximately 30° bank at the steepest point
Constant change of pitch and roll rate and airspeed
Altitude ±100 feet from entry altitude; airspeed ±10 knots from entry airspeed; heading ±10°
Continue through the number of symmetrical loops specified, then resume straight-and-level flight

callout.text: For an initial commercial ASEL applicant, the examiner must select Chandelles or Lazy Eights (ACS Appendix 3, Area V). Be ready for both.
The ACS grades the lazy eight mostly at the 180° points: same altitude, same airspeed, right heading. The top of each loop is graded by the bank: about 30°.

check.q: Where in each half of the lazy eight does the examiner check altitude, airspeed and heading, and to what tolerance?
check.a: At the 180° point: altitude ±100 feet and airspeed ±10 knots from entry, heading ±10° (ACS CA.V.D.S5c, S5d, S5e).

body.p: Symmetry comes from planning. Before you start, pick prominent reference points on the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135° from the direction in which the maneuver starts, for each 180° turn [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

head: Point
What the AFH figure shows
rows: Level flight at maneuvering or cruise speed, whichever is less, or the manufacturer's recommended speed
Bank about 30°, minimum speed, maximum altitude, pitch passing through level
Level flight, entry airspeed, entry altitude

body.p: Table source: Figure 10-4 [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

Application: the second half flies back over the same points. Start heading north and turn right: your references are toward 045, 090 and 135, and you finish heading 180. The left turn back from 180 passes 135, 090 and 045 on the way to north. So three well-chosen landmarks can serve both loops.

callout.text: Pick landmarks far away on the horizon, like a mountain, a tower or a cloud edge, not something close below you. The AFH says the reference points are on the natural horizon [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Poor choice or poor use of the 45°, 90° and 135° references, ineffective planning, and loops that are not symmetrical are all on the AFH list of common errors [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

check.q: You enter a left lazy eight heading 270. Toward what headings are your 45°, 90° and 135° references?
check.a: 225, 180 and 135 (application of the 45°, 90°, 135° rule [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]). You finish the first half heading 090.

chunks.title: The first 90°: climbing turn to the top

body.p: From level flight, start a gradual climbing turn toward the 45° reference. Plan it so the highest pitch-up attitude comes exactly at the 45° point, with about 15° of bank [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

As the nose rises, the airspeed falls, and slower airspeed makes the rate of turn go up. So start with a slow roll rate. Rising pitch plus rising bank can make the airplane turn so fast that you reach the 45° point before the highest pitch [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

Past 45°, let the pitch come down slowly toward the horizon while the bank keeps slowly increasing. At the 90° point the pitch passes through level, the bank reaches its maximum of about 30°, and the airspeed is at its minimum, about 5 to 10 knots above stall speed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

bullets: Bank is still growing between 45° and 90°, so the overbanking tendency may need a slight opposite aileron pressure at the top while you keep rudder in for the left-turning tendencies [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Rate of turn goes up as speed goes down at the same bank [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. That is why the nose sweeps across the horizon faster near the top.
The top is the slowest, highest point of the loop [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

callout.text: Do not hesitate at the 90° point. Keep the airplane moving into the descending turn [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Poor control at the top, letting the pitch fall rapidly through the horizon, is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
45: highest nose, 15° bank. 90: level nose, 30° bank, slowest. Keep everything moving.

check.q: Why should the roll into a lazy eight start slowly?
check.a: Because the airspeed is falling, the rate of turn rises; rolling in fast could carry you past the 45° point before you reach the highest pitch [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

chunks.title: The second 90°: descending turn back to level

body.p: After the 90° point, roll out of the bank slowly while you let the pitch attitude decrease. At 135° of turn the airplane should be at its lowest pitch attitude [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], with about 15° of bank [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

As the nose goes down the airspeed builds, so you need less right rudder to stay coordinated. Approaching 180°, relax rudder and aileron pressure while you bring both pitch and roll back to level. Watch how much turn is left and adjust the rollout and pitch so the wings and nose are level at the original airspeed just as you reach the 180° point [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

At the 180° point, start the climbing turn in the opposite direction right away, toward the reference points for the second half, and fly it the same way [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Continue for the number of loops the examiner asks for, then return to straight-and-level flight (ACS CA.V.D.S6).

callout.text: The 180° point is your scorecard: altitude, airspeed and heading all get checked there (ACS CA.V.D.S5c, S5d, S5e). Glance at the altimeter and airspeed at each crossing, then look back outside.
Gaining or losing altitude at each 180° point and missing the airspeed or bank standards are listed errors [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

check.q: Where is the lowest pitch attitude, and what is the bank there?
check.a: At the 135° point, with about 15° of bank [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

chunks.title: Coordination when every pressure keeps changing

body.p: The rudder's job is to keep the airplane coordinated. When you roll with aileron, the rising wing gets more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn. Rudder in the direction of the turn, applied with the aileron, cancels that adverse yaw [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

In a lazy eight a second yaw joins in. At a high angle of attack, the downward-moving propeller blade has more lift than the upward-moving one, which yaws the nose to the left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]. That is P-factor, and it grows as the airspeed falls in the climb.

bullets: Climbing and slowing: add right rudder gradually to counter P-factor, in both the right and the left loop [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Rolling right at low speed: adverse yaw and P-factor both yaw the nose left, so you need substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Rolling left: P-factor tends to cancel the adverse yaw, so you need less right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Descending and speeding up: reduce the right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Near 180°: relax rudder and aileron pressure as you level off [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

body.p: Check yourself by feel and by the ball. In a skid you feel pushed toward the outside of the turn; in a slip, toward the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. The ball shows the same thing: it moves to the inside of the turn in a slip and to the outside in a skid, and you center it with rudder on the side the ball is on, "step on the ball" [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. The AFH chandelle discussion adds glancing at the ball in the turn coordinator and using the right control pressures [[24:214|AFH 10-5]].

callout.text: Slow and rolling right: lots of right rudder. Fast and descending: let it off.
Holding uncoordinated control deflections can lead to a spin, and that is most dangerous at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

check.q: In which part of a right lazy eight is the right rudder pressure greatest, and why?
check.a: Near the top, slow and rolling right: P-factor and left adverse yaw add together [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

chunks.title: Energy management: speed for height and back

body.p: The airplane stores energy in two tanks: altitude (potential energy) and airspeed (kinetic energy). Thrust adds energy and drag takes it away [[24:87|AFH 4-1]] [[24:88|AFH 4-2]]. When you trade speed for height, the altitude goes up as the airspeed comes down; the two always move in opposite directions unless you add or remove energy [[24:88|AFH 4-2]].

The lazy eight is a long energy exchange. In the climb you pour airspeed into altitude, like row F of the figure. In the descent you pour it back. The elevator moves energy between the tanks, and the throttle changes the total. To trade speed for altitude you pitch up without first changing the throttle [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

The energy map shows lines of equal energy height. An airplane can slide along one of these lines just by exchanging speed and altitude [[24:94|AFH 4-8]]. Energy height is altitude plus V² / 2g [[24:93|AFH 4-7]]. The AFH example: 100 knots at 6,000 feet and 240 knots at 4,000 feet sit on the same 6,500-foot line [[24:94|AFH 4-8]].

Power is where the altitude standard is won or lost. With too much power for the bank you use, you finish the maneuver higher; with too little, you finish lower [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Set the power before entry so you do not exceed the manufacturer's speed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

callout.text: Application: if every 180° point is 80 feet high, the eight is adding energy. Take a little power off before the next practice set, not in the middle of a loop. The AFH gives no power numbers; your POH and CFI do.
Mismanaging altitude and airspeed contributes to the three most common fatal accident types: loss of control in flight (LOC-I), CFIT and approach-and-landing accidents [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

check.q: You keep arriving at each 180° point about 100 feet low with the airspeed on target. What does the AFH say is the likely cause?
check.a: Too little power for the bank angle used; insufficient power loses altitude [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

body.p: Enter at the manufacturer's recommended speed. The AFH says the entry speed is generally no greater than VA or VO [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], and Figure 10-4 labels the entry as maneuvering or cruise speed, whichever is less, or the manufacturer's speed [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. The PHAK says the recommended entry speed for chandelles and lazy eights is generally near the design maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

VA is the highest speed at which the structure's limit load can be put on the airplane, by gusts or full control deflection, without damage. It changes with weight: perhaps 100 knots heavy but only 90 knots light [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. VA is not marked on the airspeed indicator; like some other limits, it is found on placards and in the AFM/POH [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

The colored arcs still matter. The bottom of the green arc (VS1) is the clean stall speed at maximum takeoff weight for most airplanes, and the yellow arc is for smooth air only and with caution [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]]. Application: at the top of each loop you are near the bottom of the green arc, and as each loop ends you are heading back toward entry speed.

The Vg diagram puts it together. The airplane must stay inside an envelope that does not pass the redline, does not pass the limit load factor, and cannot pass the maximum lift line, because above that line it stalls [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]. The most load factor the wing can make goes up with the square of the airspeed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. So at the slow top of a lazy eight the wing has very little load factor to spare before it stalls.

callout.text: The configuration, power and airspeed must be the recommended ones (ACS CA.V.D.S3). The AFH chandelle entry is flaps and gear up [[24:214|AFH 10-5]]; for the lazy eight, check your POH.

check.q: Name two airspeed limitations that you will not find marked on the airspeed indicator.
check.a: For example VA and the landing gear speeds VLO and VLE; they are on placards and in the AFM/POH [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

chunks.title: Load factor and the accelerated stall at the top

body.p: Any stall with more than +1 G on the airplane is an accelerated maneuver stall, and it happens at a higher indicated airspeed than the normal stall. It usually comes from a turn, a pull-up or an abrupt change in flightpath [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. The slow, banked, nose-high top of a lazy eight is exactly where a hard pull can find one.

Application of the square-root rule [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]: a level 30° bank needs a load factor of 1 / cos 30° = 1.15, which raises the stall speed by about 7 percent. An airplane that stalls at 52 knots would stall near 56 knots in a level 30° turn, and the AFH puts the top of the loop only 5 to 10 knots above the stall [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. The margin is thin.

The PHAK says load factors in lazy eights depend on how fast the dives are and how abrupt the pull-ups are. The better the maneuver, the lower the load factor. A pull-up above 2 G gains less altitude, and in low-powered airplanes it can even cause a net loss of altitude [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

bullets: Stalls from abrupt maneuvers tend to be more aggressive than 1 G stalls and can come at higher speeds or lower pitch attitudes than you expect [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
If the airplane is uncoordinated at the stall, the bank may change until the angle of attack is reduced [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Recovery: forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack and stop the stall warning, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Failing to recover at once can lead to a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Stalling at any point in the maneuver is a listed common error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. If the buffet or stall warning comes at the top, unload first. A lost loop is far better than a spin.
Smooth pull, small G. Big pull, big stall speed.

check.q: What is the first action if the stall warning sounds at the top of a loop?
check.a: Forward elevator pressure to reduce the angle of attack, then level the wings, coordinate with rudder and adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

chunks.title: Clearing the area and collision hazards

body.p: A clearing turn makes sure the next maneuver will not take you into another airplane's path. Clear before all turns and every training maneuver; clearing plus good scanning is the most effective way to avoid a collision [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

bullets: During training, make clearing turns before the maneuver and say the clearing calls out loud: clear left, right, above and below [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Scan with short, regular eye movements, each no more than 10° and held at least 1 second [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
Use the horizon to judge another airplane's altitude: above it, probably higher than you; below it, probably lower [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Move your head to see past door posts and wings; sometimes lift a wing to look [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].
Haze, smoke and flying toward the sun cut your ability to see traffic, and a dirty windshield hides it [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

body.p: A lazy eight is hard on your scan. It climbs and descends through several hundred feet, it sweeps through 180° each way, and the high wing and nose-high attitude hide parts of the sky. Not scanning for traffic during the maneuver is on the AFH error list [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

callout.text: Application: before each new pair of loops, take a fresh look in the direction of the next turn and above you, since the next climb will take you there.

check.q: What does the PHAK want you to say during clearing turns in training?

body.p: The ACS requires an altitude that lets you fly the whole maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.D.S2). The lowest part of a lazy eight is near the 180° points, where you should be back at entry altitude [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], and the ACS lets that point be up to 100 feet low (ACS CA.V.D.S5c). Plan for it.
Remember your altimeter shows height above sea level, not above the ground [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Look up the highest terrain and obstacles in the practice area before you pick the entry altitude.

Why the margin matters: maneuvering is the most common phase of flight for general aviation LOC-I accidents [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]. A stall or spin from a slow, banked attitude needs room, and mismanaged energy near the ground leads to CFIT [[24:87|AFH 4-1]]. Uncoordinated flight is most hazardous at low altitude [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

callout.text: The 1,500-foot figure also appears in 14 CFR 91.303 for aerobatic flight, which means an intentional maneuver with an abrupt change in attitude, an abnormal attitude or abnormal acceleration not needed for normal flight [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]. The sources do not call the lazy eight aerobatic; the 1,500-foot AGL floor here comes from the ACS.

With a passenger who is not a crewmember and no parachutes, no intentional maneuver may exceed 60° of bank or 30° nose up or down. Flight tests and required maneuvers given by a CFI are excepted [[60:506|14 CFR 91.307]].

check.q: Terrain under the practice area is 1,200 feet MSL. What is the lowest entry altitude that keeps even a 100-foot low 180° point at 1,500 feet AGL or above?
check.a: 2,800 feet MSL: 1,200 + 1,500 = 2,700, plus 100 feet of allowed error (ACS CA.V.D.S2, S5c). Application: add more margin than that.

chunks.title: Division of attention, distractions and disorientation

body.p: In a lazy eight you are flying a moving target. Pitch, bank, airspeed and rudder all change at the same time, you track three reference points, and you keep scanning for traffic. The AFH says performance maneuvers exist to build division of attention [[24:210|AFH 10-1]].

Fly it by looking outside. About 90 percent of your attention should be on outside references and traffic, and no more than about 10 percent inside [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. Flying the lazy eight by the instruments instead of visual references is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

bullets: Distraction and fixation crowd out the tasks that matter most [[24:51|AFH 2-14]].
Many airplane upsets begin while the pilot's attention is taken away from the flight instruments or outside references [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Avoid sudden, extreme head movements during long turns; they can set off the Coriolis illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
A sloping cloud deck or an obscured horizon can create a false horizon [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Pick reference points on a clear natural horizon.
An abrupt change from climb to level flight can create the inversion illusion, a feeling of tumbling backward [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Smooth pitch changes help.

callout.text: Task priority: attitude and coordination first, the next reference point second, the instruments only at the 180° points. If something distracts you mid-loop, finish to the 180° point and roll out level.

check.q: About how much of your attention should be inside the cockpit during a visual maneuver like the lazy eight?

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH and CFI give the real speeds and power setting.

bullets: 1. Pick an altitude that keeps the whole maneuver at or above 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.D.S2).
2. Clear the area with clearing turns and a spoken scan (ACS CA.V.D.S1) [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
3. Choose reference points on the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135° for each half [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
4. Set the recommended configuration, power and entry airspeed, generally no more than VA or VO (ACS CA.V.D.S3) [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
5. From level flight, start a slow, gradual climbing turn so the highest pitch comes at 45° with about 15° of bank [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

6. Let the nose come down toward the horizon while the bank keeps growing; at 90° the pitch passes level, the bank is about 30° and the speed is lowest. Add right rudder as you slow [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
7. Without pausing, roll out slowly and let the nose drop to its lowest point at 135°, easing off right rudder as you speed up [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
8. Time the rollout so wings and nose are level at entry airspeed and altitude exactly at 180° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
9. Start the climbing turn the other way at once and fly the second half the same way [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
10. After the loops the examiner asks for, return to straight-and-level flight (ACS CA.V.D.S6).

body.p: Smoothness is graded. The ACS asks for a constant change of pitch and roll rate and airspeed (ACS CA.V.D.S5b). There is no moment in a good lazy eight when everything is held still.

callout.text: Climb to 45, level at 90, lowest at 135, level at 180, then turn the other way.

check.q: At which point of the loop is the bank steepest, and what does the ACS want it to be?

body.p: The AFH lists thirteen common errors for lazy eights [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Here is what each looks like and how to fix it.

head: AFH common error
What it looks like
Fix
rows: One loop tall and narrow, the other flat
Same pitch and bank at the same reference points each way [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Poor selection or use of references
Pick far, prominent points on the natural horizon [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Highest pitch reached late, after the 45° point
Slow, steady roll rate at the start [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Altitude gained or lost at each 180°
Adjust the power for the next set: excess power gains, too little loses [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Nose drops fast through the horizon
Keep the roll and pitch moving smoothly at 90° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Airspeed or bank standards not met
Bank well past 30°, speed off at 180°
Fly to the reference points; check speed at each 180° point [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Right rudder with falling speed, less as it builds [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Buffet or horn at the top
Less pitch-up at 45°, smooth pull, recover at once [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]
Steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver
Lead with pitch; bank only about 15° at 45° [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]

body.p: Table source: the common error list [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; fixes as cited.

callout.text: The most dangerous error is a stall at the slow top while uncoordinated. Keep the ball centered there above all.
Commercial standard reminder: about 30° of bank at the steepest point; at each 180° point, altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, heading ±10° (ACS CA.V.D.S5).

check.q: Your lazy eight looks like a steep turn with a bit of climb. What is wrong?
check.a: Too much bank and too little pitch change; 'execution of a steep turn instead of a climbing maneuver' is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Lead with pitch and hold about 15° of bank at 45° [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

f1.alt: A light airplane flies a blue ribbon path across a road in the countryside. Starting at A in level flight, it climbs in a turn past B at the 45° point, reaches the top at C at the 90° point with about 30° of bank, descends past D at the 135° point, and is level again at E at the 180° point before turning the other way. Yellow boxes list pitch, bank, speed and altitude at each point.

f2.caption: Figure 3-12. The rudder opposes adverse yaw to help coordinate the turn. (AFH 3-13)
f2.alt: A light airplane rolling into a left turn over a town. The rising right wing has a large More lift arrow and additional induced drag; the lowered left wing has a Reduced lift arrow. A red arrow at the nose shows adverse yaw, and a box says the rudder opposes adverse yaw to coordinate the turn.

f3.caption: Figure 5-51. Asymmetrical loading of propeller (P-factor). (PHAK 5-33)
f3.alt: Two side views of an airplane nose. At low angle of attack the load arrows on the upward and downward moving propeller blades are equal. At high angle of attack the airplane is nose high and the arrow on the downward moving blade is larger than the one on the upward moving blade.

f4.caption: Figure 4-1 A-F. Examples of typical energy transactions. (AFH 4-2)
f4.alt: Six rows labeled A to F. Each shows a tank split into stored altitude (blue) and stored airspeed (gold), with a thrust arrow T in and a drag arrow D out, and a net energy change column. In A and B thrust exceeds drag; in C and D drag exceeds thrust; in E and F thrust equals drag. Row F shows a curved arrow moving energy from the airspeed side into the altitude side.

f5.caption: Figure 4-6. The altitude-speed "map" showing lines of constant energy height. (AFH 4-7)
f5.alt: A graph of altitude from 0 to 16,000 feet against airspeed from 0 to 350 knots, with curved dotted lines of constant energy height labeled 2,000 to 11,000 feet. Point A at 100 knots and 6,000 feet and point B at about 240 knots and 4,000 feet lie on the same 6,500-foot line.

f6.caption: Figure 5-55. Typical Vg diagram. (PHAK 5-38)
f6.alt: A graph of load factor from minus 3 to 7 against indicated airspeed in mph. A red curve rises from the normal stall speed at 1 G near 64 mph along the accelerated stall line to maneuvering speed at about 4.4 G. A green normal operating range runs to maximum structural cruising speed, a yellow caution range to the never-exceed speed near 225 mph, with structural damage and failure areas beyond.

f7.caption: Figure 8-8. Single engine airspeed indicator (ASI). (PHAK 8-9)
f7.alt: An airspeed indicator in knots with a white arc from VS0 to VFE, a green arc from VS1 to VNO, a yellow arc from VNO to the red line at VNE, each labeled with an orange box and arrow.

scenario.title: Hazy afternoon, light airplane, lazy eights on the checkride
scenario.setup: You are on a commercial checkride in a four-seat fixed-gear single. It is just you and the examiner with half fuel, so you are well below maximum weight. The practice area is over rolling farmland with terrain near 1,100 feet MSL and a few towers. A thin haze sits over the area and a sloping cloud deck lies to the east. The examiner asks for lazy eights, two loops, starting to the right.

questions.q: How do you choose your entry altitude?
questions.a: High enough that the whole maneuver, including a 180° point up to 100 feet low, stays at or above 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.D.S2, S5c), based on the highest terrain and towers, since the altimeter reads MSL, not AGL [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

questions.q: What entry speed do you use, given the light weight?
questions.a: The POH's recommended entry speed, generally no greater than VA or VO [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. VA drops as weight drops, so use the value for today's lighter weight [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

questions.q: Where do you place your reference points, and what about the clouds to the east?
questions.a: On the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135° from the entry heading [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Avoid using the sloping cloud deck as a horizon; it can create a false horizon illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

questions.q: Near the top of the first right loop the ball slides left and you feel pushed to the left. What is happening and what do you do?
questions.a: You feel pushed toward the outside of the right turn and the ball is to the outside, so it is a skid [[24:74|AFH 3-13]] [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. Step on the ball: ease off the right rudder (left rudder pressure) until the ball centers [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. Slow and rolling right normally needs substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], so make the change small and check the ball again.

questions.q: At the top of the second loop the stall horn chirps and the buffet starts. What now?
questions.a: This is an accelerated stall warning. Reduce the angle of attack with forward elevator, level the wings with aileron, coordinate with rudder, and adjust power [[24:125|AFH 5-20]]. Stalling at any point is a listed error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; a safe recovery comes first.

questions.q: On the debrief the examiner notes you ended both loops 90 feet high. What do you change next time?
questions.a: Use slightly less power for the bank you are flying; excess power for a given bank gains altitude by the end of the maneuver [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. You were inside ±100 feet (ACS CA.V.D.S5c), but close to the limit.

skills.do: Clear the area before the maneuver.
skills.practice: Fly clearing turns before every set of loops and say 'clear left, right, above, and below' out loud [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]] [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].

skills.do: Pick an altitude that lets you fly the whole maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL.
skills.practice: Before the flight, find the highest terrain in the practice area and add 1,500 feet plus a margin for the ±100-foot tolerance (ACS CA.V.D.S5c).

skills.do: Set the recommended entry configuration, power and airspeed.
skills.practice: Brief the POH entry speed (generally no more than VA or VO for today's weight) and your power setting before takeoff [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

skills.do: Stay coordinated through the whole maneuver.
skills.practice: Say 'right rudder' out loud as the speed falls and 'ease off' as it builds, then check the ball at 45°, 90°, 135° and 180° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: Reach approximately 30° of bank at the steepest point.
skills.practice: Learn the 30° sight picture of the wings on the horizon and arrive at it exactly at the 90° reference [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: Keep pitch, roll rate and airspeed changing constantly, with no pauses or jerks.
skills.practice: Fly a few loops calling out each reference point as it passes, so you notice any point where the nose or wings stop moving.

skills.do: Arrive at each 180° point within 100 feet of the entry altitude.
skills.practice: Note the altimeter at each 180° point and adjust power for the next set: more power gains altitude, less loses it [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: Arrive at each 180° point within 10 knots of the entry airspeed.
skills.practice: Time the descent so the nose comes level just as the speed returns to entry speed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: Arrive at each 180° point within 10° of the planned heading.
skills.practice: Watch how much turn is left and adjust the rollout rate to finish level on the 180° heading [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: Fly the number of symmetrical loops the examiner asks for, then return to straight-and-level flight.
skills.practice: Practice at least two full eights in a row, comparing pitch and bank at the same reference points in each loop [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: What does the commercial ACS require for bank angle in a lazy eight?
options: Approximately 15° at the 45° point
Approximately 30° at the steepest point
Approximately 45° at the 90° point
No more than 20° at any point
quiz.why: The ACS asks for approximately 30° of bank at the steepest point (ACS CA.V.D.S5a), which the AFH places at the 90° point [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: In each 180° half of a lazy eight, what does the airplane do?
options: Descends in the first 90° and climbs in the second
Climbs in the first 90° and descends in the second
Climbs for the whole 180°
Holds altitude and changes only bank
quiz.why: The first 90° is a climb and the second 90° is a descent [[24:215|AFH 10-6]].

quiz.q: At what point should the maximum pitch-up attitude occur?
options: At the 45° point
At the 90° point
At the 135° point
At the 180° point
quiz.why: The climbing turn is planned so the maximum pitch-up attitude is reached at the 45° point, with about 15° of bank [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: What is the airspeed at the 90° point, according to the AFH?
options: Entry airspeed
About 5 to 10 knots above stall speed
Exactly the stall speed
Halfway between entry speed and VA
quiz.why: At the 90° point the airspeed is at its minimum, about 5 to 10 knots above stall speed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: As the airspeed decreases in the climbing turn, what does the pilot do with the rudder?
options: Gradually add right rudder pressure
Gradually add left rudder pressure
Neutralize the rudder
Use rudder only to raise the nose
quiz.why: As the airspeed decreases, right rudder pressure is gradually applied to counter left-turning tendencies such as P-factor [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: In the energy view, which control mainly moves energy between altitude and airspeed?
options: The throttle
The elevator
The rudder
The mixture
quiz.why: The throttle adds or removes total energy, while the elevator distributes it between altitude and airspeed [[24:95|AFH 4-9]] [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

quiz.q: Where do you find VA, the design maneuvering speed?
options: As the top of the green arc
As the yellow arc
On placards and in the AFM/POH, not on the airspeed indicator
As a blue line on the airspeed indicator
quiz.why: Some airspeed limitations, such as VA, are not marked on the ASI but are found on placards and in the AFM/POH [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]] [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

quiz.q: What does the PHAK say about a lazy eight flown with a pull-up above 2 G?
options: It gains the most altitude
It gains less altitude and may even lose altitude in a low-powered airplane
It is required to meet the ACS
It has no effect on altitude
quiz.why: A pull-up producing more than 2 G will not give as great a gain in altitude, and in low-powered aircraft may cause a net loss [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

quiz.q: Which statement about an accelerated maneuver stall is true?
options: It can only happen at 1 G
It happens at a higher indicated airspeed than the 1 G stall
It can only happen with flaps extended
It always happens at the same pitch attitude as a normal stall
quiz.why: Stalls with more than +1 G are accelerated maneuver stalls and happen at a higher indicated airspeed [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

quiz.q: Which illusion can an abrupt change from climb to level flight create?
options: The leans
Inversion illusion
Autokinesis
Elevator illusion
quiz.why: An abrupt change from climb to straight and level can create the illusion of tumbling backwards, the inversion illusion [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

final_quiz.q: At the first 180° point you are 120 feet above entry altitude, 6 knots fast and 5° off heading. What fails the commercial standard?
options: The altitude
The airspeed
The heading
Nothing; all are within tolerance
final_quiz.why: At the 180° point the ACS allows altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots and heading ±10° (ACS CA.V.D.S5c, S5d, S5e). 120 feet is outside. AFH lists gain or loss of altitude at each 180 degree point as a lazy eight error [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: You reach the 45° reference point while the nose is still rising toward its highest pitch. What is the most likely cause?
options: The roll rate at entry was too fast
The entry speed was too slow
Too much right rudder
The power was set too low
final_quiz.why: Increasing pitch and bank together make the rate of turn rapid, so a fast roll can carry you to the 45° point before the highest pitch. Start with a slow roll rate [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: During a left lazy eight, compared with a right one, how does the rudder needed while rolling at low speed differ?
options: Much more right rudder, because P-factor and adverse yaw add
Less right rudder, because P-factor tends to cancel the adverse yaw
Left rudder only, because P-factor reverses
No difference; rudder is the same both ways
final_quiz.why: In left climbing turns or rolling left, left-yawing P-factor tends to cancel the adverse yaw to the right, so less right rudder is needed. Rolling right at low speed and high power needs substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: Your 180° points keep coming out 80 to 100 feet high, but airspeed and heading are fine. Which change fits the AFH?
options: Steepen the bank at 90° to 45°
Use slightly less power for the bank angle
Pull harder at the 45° point
Enter 20 knots faster
final_quiz.why: If excess power is used for a given bank angle, altitude is gained by the end of the maneuver [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Steepening past about 30° breaks the bank standard (ACS CA.V.D.S5a).

final_quiz.q: Using the AFH energy map, an airplane at 100 knots and 6,000 feet has the same energy height as one at about 240 knots and 4,000 feet. What does that mean?
options: Both are at 6,000 feet
Both could zoom to the same maximum altitude by trading all their speed
The faster one has more total energy
The slower one needs more power to stay level
final_quiz.why: Points on the same energy-height line have the same total energy and could zoom to the same maximum altitude, here 6,500 feet [[24:94|AFH 4-8]].

final_quiz.q: In the AFH energy rules, how do you trade airspeed for altitude?
options: Increase throttle and pitch down
Pitch up without first changing the throttle
Reduce throttle and pitch up
Increase throttle and hold pitch
final_quiz.why: Rule 3: to exchange energy, do not change the throttle at first; pitch up to trade speed for altitude [[24:96|AFH 4-10]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 knots at 1 G. At 60 knots near the top of a loop, what is the most load factor the wing can make before it stalls?
options: About 1.2 G
About 1.44 G
About 2.0 G
About 3.8 G
final_quiz.why: The maximum load factor varies with the square of the airspeed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]: (60 / 50)² = 1.2² = 1.44 G. A level 30° bank already needs about 1.15 G.

final_quiz.q: Why is the cross-control stall especially dangerous?
options: It always happens at high altitude
It can come with little warning and roll the airplane toward inverted, the start of a spin
It only happens with flaps down
It gives a long, gentle buffet
final_quiz.why: The cross-control stall can occur with very little warning; the nose may drop, the bank may change suddenly, and the airplane may roll to inverted, usually the beginning of a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

final_quiz.q: According to the AFH, what upset parameter does a well-flown lazy eight stay well inside?
options: Bank angle greater than 45°
Bank angle greater than 20°
Pitch attitude greater than 5° nose up
Airspeed below VY
final_quiz.why: The FAA upset parameters include pitch more than 25° nose up, more than 10° nose down, and bank more than 45° [[24:106|AFH 5-1]]. The lazy eight's bank peaks at about 30° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

final_quiz.q: 14 CFR 91.303 prohibits aerobatic flight below what height above the surface?
options: 1,000 feet
1,500 feet
2,000 feet
3,000 feet
final_quiz.why: No aerobatic flight below an altitude of 1,500 feet above the surface [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]. The lazy eight floor of 1,500 feet AGL comes from the ACS (ACS CA.V.D.S2).

final_quiz.q: You plan lazy eight practice on a clear day. Which spot does the AIM name as a place where aircraft tend to cluster?
options: Over open farmland far from airports
Airways, especially near VORs, and Class B, C, D and E surface areas
Above 10,000 feet MSL
Over large bodies of water
final_quiz.why: Airways, especially near VORs, and Class B, C, D and E surface areas are high hazard areas, and most collisions happen in good weather [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

final_quiz.q: On a hazy day you see another airplane slightly below the horizon. What does the AIM suggest about its altitude?
options: It is probably higher than you
It is probably lower than you
It is at your altitude
Nothing can be judged from the horizon
final_quiz.why: Use the horizon as a reference: an aircraft below the horizon is probably flying lower [[34:188|AIM 8-1-8]].

final_quiz.q: If you pull hard in a lazy eight, what does the AIM say happens in the pilot's body?
options: Blood shifts toward the head, causing red-out
Blood shifts toward the lower body, and enough of it can narrow vision toward gray-out
No effect below 3 G
The inner ear senses level flight
final_quiz.why: In pull-ups and steep turns, blood and organs shift toward the lower body; the symptoms progress through narrowing vision, gray-out and black-out [[34:187|AIM 8-1-7]]. A smooth lazy eight keeps G low [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

takeaways: Commercial standard: about 30° of bank at the steepest point; at each 180° point, altitude ±100 feet, airspeed ±10 knots, heading ±10°.
Highest pitch at 45° (about 15° of bank), level pitch and about 30° of bank at 90°, lowest pitch at 135°, level at 180°.
Pick reference points on the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135°; they serve both halves.
Right rudder grows as the speed falls, most when rolling right slow; ease it off as the speed builds.
The lazy eight is an energy exchange; power sets whether you finish high or low.
The slow top is where an accelerated stall waits: smooth pulls, low G.
Clear the area, stay at or above 1,500 feet AGL, and fly it by looking outside.
cfi_notes: The AFH text and Figure 10-4 put about 15° of bank at both the 45° and 135° points and about 30° at 90° [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] [[24:215|AFH 10-6]]. The ACS checks only the 30° figure (ACS CA.V.D.S5a). Teach the 15° marks as a sight-picture aid, not a test item.

The entry speed wording differs slightly: the AFH text says generally no greater than VA or VO [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], Figure 10-4 says maneuvering or cruise speed whichever is less, or the manufacturer's speed [[24:215|AFH 10-6]], and the PHAK says generally near design maneuvering speed [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. They agree on the ceiling; teach the POH speed for the day's weight.

PHAK 5-36 gives 4 G for a high-speed stall at 112 knots in an airplane that stalls at 60 knots [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Working the same case with the square-of-airspeed rule on PHAK 5-37 [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]] gives (112 / 60)² = 3.5 G. If a student works the numbers, use the rule and expect the difference.

PHAK 5-37 says that below maneuvering speed no combination of maneuver and gust can cause damage [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]], but PHAK 5-36 warns that large alternating control inputs can cause structural failure at any speed, including below VA [[1:133|PHAK 5-36]]. Teach the more cautious wording.

PHAK 5-37 calls the Vg diagram Figure 5-55 in one sentence and Figure 5-53 in the next paragraph [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]]. The Vg diagram printed on PHAK 5-38 is Figure 5-55 [[1:135|PHAK 5-38]]; Figure 5-53 is the bank angle and load factor chart on PHAK 5-34 [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]]. Point students to Figure 5-55.

The rudder paragraph on AFH 10-7 is hard to follow. Boil it down the way the AFH does at its end: rolling right at low airspeed and high power takes substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Then let the ball confirm it.

Students often fly the top as a pause. Use the AFH line that the pilot should not hesitate at the 90° point [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], and call 'keep it moving' at each reference point on the first few sets.
Have the student say each reference point out loud ('45, highest; 90, level, 30; 135, lowest; 180, level') so you can hear whether the plan and the airplane match.
If the student finishes high or low, change the power between sets, not in the middle of a loop [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
gaps: The sources give no pitch attitude numbers for the 45° and 135° points; the right pitch depends on the airplane, power and entry speed. Work it out with your CFI.

The sources give no power setting for the lazy eight beyond not exceeding the manufacturer's entry speed and the effect of excess or insufficient power [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Get the power setting from the POH or your CFI.

The stall speed in the 'about 5 to 10 knots above stall speed' line [[24:216|AFH 10-7]] is not defined (1 G stall or accelerated stall at 30° of bank). Ask your CFI which your airplane's numbers mean.
No source here says whether a lazy eight counts as aerobatic flight under 14 CFR 91.303 [[60:505|14 CFR 91.303]]; the 1,500-foot AGL floor in this lesson comes from the ACS.
Entry configuration (flaps, cowl flaps, mixture) for the lazy eight is not spelled out in the AFH; it comes from the POH (ACS CA.V.D.S3).

activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin on the row it describes.

activities.title: More right rudder or less?
activities.intro: Tap each moment in the lazy eight, then tap the rudder change it needs.

items.t: At the apex of a left loop, compared with entry speed
Rolling right at low airspeed and high power
Nose coming down and airspeed building after the 90° point
Rolling left in a left climbing turn, compared with rolling right
Approaching the 180° point and leveling off, compared with the slow apex
Slowest point near the apex, compared with entry speed

activities.title: Work the lazy eight numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Ignoring drag and power changes, how much altitude could you gain by trading airspeed from 105 knots to 60 knots? Use energy height h + V² / 2g, with 1 knot = 1.688 ft/s and g = 32.17 ft/s². Round to the nearest foot.

Your airplane stalls at 48 knots at 1 G. What is its stall speed in a level, coordinated 30° bank? Load factor in a level turn = 1 / cos(bank), and stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor. Round to the nearest knot.
items.why: Load factor = 1 / cos 30° = 1.155. Square root = 1.075. 48 x 1.075 = 51.6, about 52 knots. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

items.q: At the top of the loop you are at 60 knots TAS with 30° of bank. Using ROT = 1,091 x tan(bank) / TAS in knots, what is your rate of turn?
Near entry you are at 105 knots TAS with 15° of bank. Using ROT = 1,091 x tan(bank) / TAS in knots, what is your rate of turn?
items.why: ROT = 1,091 x tan 15° / 105 = 1,091 x 0.2679 / 105 = 2.78° per second, almost four times slower than at the top [[1:136|PHAK 5-39]].

items.q: You start a right lazy eight heading 060. After the first 180° of turn, you turn back to the left. Toward what heading is your 45° reference in the second half?
items.why: The first half ends heading 060 + 180 = 240. Turning left from 240, the 45° reference is 240 - 45 = 195, the same point as the 135° reference of the first half (060 + 135 = 195) [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

items.q: The highest terrain and obstacles in the area reach 1,900 feet MSL. The 180° points are the lowest points of the maneuver. What is the lowest entry altitude that keeps a 180° point flown 100 feet low at 1,500 feet AGL?
items.why: 1,900 + 1,500 = 3,400 feet MSL for the lowest point; the 180° point may be 100 feet below entry, so enter at 3,400 + 100 = 3,500 feet MSL or higher (ACS CA.V.D.S2, S5c).

activities.title: True or false: limits and loads
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The lazy eight is the only standard training maneuver in which flight control pressures are constantly changing.
The upper limit of the green arc is VA, the design maneuvering speed.
cards.why: False. The top of the green arc is VNO, maximum structural cruising speed; VA is not marked on the ASI [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

cards.s: The most load factor the wing can make before stalling goes up with the square of the airspeed.
In a lazy eight, the better the maneuver is flown, the lower the load factor.
cards.why: True. The PHAK says the better the maneuver is performed, the less extreme the load factor [[1:134|PHAK 5-37]].

cards.s: The yellow arc on the airspeed indicator is for use in any air, as long as you are careful.
cards.why: False. Fly in the yellow arc only in smooth air, and then only with caution [[1:211|PHAK 8-9]].

cards.s: Indicated altitude and its potential energy are measured above mean sea level, not above the ground.
cards.why: True. The pilot's energy frame of reference is indicated altitude above MSL and indicated airspeed [[24:87|AFH 4-1]].

activities.title: Put one half of the lazy eight in order

steps: Clear the area and confirm the altitude keeps you at or above 1,500 feet AGL
Pick reference points at 45°, 90° and 135° and set the entry power and airspeed

Let the nose come down to level at 90° with about 30° of bank and the lowest speed
Roll out slowly as the nose drops to its lowest point at 135°
Arrive level at entry altitude and airspeed at 180°
Start the climbing turn the other way at once

activities.title: Lazy eights, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are practicing lazy eights with your CFI before your commercial checkride. You are light today, the practice area terrain is about 1,000 feet MSL, and the air is smooth. Your CFI asks for two loops, starting to the left.

steps.s: You are level at 2,500 feet MSL, cleared, and ready to start.
options: Start now; 1,500 feet AGL at entry is enough
Climb so even a 180° point flown 100 feet low stays at or above 1,500 feet AGL
Descend to 2,000 feet for better references
Start, and climb if the first loop goes low
steps.why: 2,500 - 1,000 = 1,500 feet AGL at entry, so a 180° point flown even 50 feet low would put you below 1,500 feet AGL. The ACS requires the whole maneuver no lower than 1,500 feet AGL (ACS CA.V.D.S2, S5c).

steps.s: Now at a safe altitude, you look for reference points. Low clouds slope across the horizon to the south.
options: Use the cloud edges as the horizon
Pick distant ground landmarks on the natural horizon at 45°, 90° and 135°
Use the heading indicator only
Skip references and fly by feel
steps.why: Reference points belong on the natural horizon [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Sloping clouds can create a false horizon [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

steps.s: Passing the 90° point of the first loop: bank 30°, nose passing through level, airspeed 8 knots above stall. The bank wants to keep steepening.
options: Pause here for a moment to let the airspeed settle
Hold slight opposite aileron against the overbanking, keep the rudder pressure in, and keep going into the descending turn
Pull back to hold the nose on the horizon a little longer
Release all rudder pressure, since the climb is over
steps.why: At the 90° point a slight opposite aileron pressure may be needed to stop overbanking while rudder still cancels the left-turning tendencies, and the pilot should not hesitate there [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Pulling at this low speed invites an accelerated stall [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

steps.s: At the top of the second loop, rolling right, the airspeed is very low and the ball is well to the right.
options: Add left rudder
Add right rudder to center the ball
Add right aileron to steepen the bank
Pull back to raise the nose
steps.why: The ball to the inside of a right turn is a slip; step on the ball, so add right rudder [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. More bank would make the slip worse [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]. Rolling right at low airspeed and high power needs substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

steps.s: Both 180° points came out 110 feet low with airspeed on target.
options: Steepen the bank to 40° next time
Add a little power for the next set
Enter 15 knots above VA
Ignore it; altitude is not graded
steps.why: Insufficient power for a given bank loses altitude [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], and 110 feet is outside ±100 feet (ACS CA.V.D.S5c). VA is a ceiling for entry speed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
